blocks.body:
The spectral theorem gives a beautiful picture of a symmetric matrix: a stretch along perpendicular axes. Most matrices are not symmetric, and many are not even square. A $1000\times 800$ matrix of pixel brightnesses, or of ratings that users gave to films, has no eigenvalues at all. Is there still a simple picture?

There is, and it is almost as simple. Any matrix $A$ maps some orthonormal set of input directions to perpendicular output directions, stretched by factors $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \cdots \ge 0$. The only difference from the symmetric case is that the output axes need not be the same as the input axes. This is the singular value decomposition, and it is one of the most useful factorisations in applied mathematics.

blocks.title: A picture in two dimensions
blocks.body:
Take $A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0\\ 4 & 5\end{pmatrix}$. It sends the unit circle to an ellipse. Which unit vectors $x$ are stretched the most? The squared length is
$$\|Ax\|^2 = x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Ax,$$
a quadratic form in the symmetric matrix $A^{\mathsf T}A = \begin{pmatrix} 25 & 20\\ 20 & 25\end{pmatrix}$. By the Rayleigh principle of [[spectral-theorem]], its maximum on the unit circle is the largest eigenvalue $45$, attained at $x = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1)$, and its minimum is $5$, at $x = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1)$. So the ellipse has semi-axes of length $\sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt5$ and $\sqrt5$, and $3\sqrt5 \cdot \sqrt5 = 15 = |\det A|$, the area-scaling factor.

The key observation is that the images of these two directions are perpendicular: $A(1, 1) = (3, 9)$ and $A(1, -1) = (3, -1)$, and $3\cdot 3 + 9\cdot(-1) = 0$. So $A$ takes one pair of perpendicular directions to another pair of perpendicular directions, stretching by $3\sqrt5$ and $\sqrt5$. This is no accident, as the proof below shows, and it works for every matrix.

blocks.title: Singular value decomposition
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a real $m\times n$ matrix of rank $r$. There are orthonormal bases $v_1, \dots, v_n$ of $\mathbb R^n$ and $u_1, \dots, u_m$ of $\mathbb R^m$, and numbers $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \cdots \ge \sigma_r > 0$, such that
$$Av_i = \sigma_iu_i \ (i \le r), \qquad Av_i = 0 \ (i > r).$$
In matrix form, $A = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}$, where $U$ and $V$ are the orthogonal matrices with columns $u_i$ and $v_i$, and $\Sigma$ is the $m\times n$ matrix with $\Sigma_{ii} = \sigma_i$ for $i \le r$ and all other entries $0$. The numbers $\sigma_i$, the singular values, are the square roots of the nonzero eigenvalues of $A^{\mathsf T}A$, and hence are uniquely determined by $A$.

The matrix $A^{\mathsf T}A$ is $n\times n$ and symmetric, and it has no negative eigenvalues: if $A^{\mathsf T}Ax = \lambda x$ with $\|x\| = 1$, then $\lambda = x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Ax = \|Ax\|^2 \ge 0$. By the spectral theorem there is an orthonormal basis $v_1, \dots, v_n$ of $\mathbb R^n$ with $A^{\mathsf T}Av_i = \lambda_iv_i$, ordered so that $\lambda_1 \ge \cdots \ge \lambda_n \ge 0$.

Let $s$ be the number of positive $\lambda_i$, and for $i \le s$ put $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$ and $u_i = Av_i/\sigma_i$. These $u_i$ are orthonormal:
$$\langle u_i, u_j\rangle = \frac{v_i^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Av_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j} = \frac{\lambda_j\langle v_i, v_j\rangle}{\sigma_i\sigma_j},$$
which is $1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise. For $i > s$ we have $\|Av_i\|^2 = \lambda_i = 0$, so $Av_i = 0$.

The image of $A$ is spanned by the images $Av_1, \dots, Av_n$ of a basis, that is by $u_1, \dots, u_s$; being orthonormal, these are a basis of the image, so $s = \operatorname{rank} A = r$. Extend $u_1, \dots, u_r$ to an orthonormal basis $u_1, \dots, u_m$ of $\mathbb R^m$ (Gram–Schmidt, [[inner-products]]). Then $Av_i = \sigma_iu_i$ for $i \le r$ and $Av_i = 0$ otherwise, which says $AV = U\Sigma$ column by column. Since $V^{-1} = V^{\mathsf T}$, this is $A = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}$.

Uniqueness of the $\sigma_i$: from any such factorisation, $A^{\mathsf T}A = V\Sigma^{\mathsf T}\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}$, so $A^{\mathsf T}A$ is similar to the diagonal matrix $\Sigma^{\mathsf T}\Sigma$ with entries $\sigma_1^2, \dots, \sigma_r^2, 0, \dots, 0$. These are therefore its eigenvalues.

blocks.title: What the SVD tells you
blocks.body:
Multiplying out $U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}$ gives the SVD as a sum of rank-one pieces,
$$A = \sigma_1u_1v_1^{\mathsf T} + \sigma_2u_2v_2^{\mathsf T} + \cdots + \sigma_ru_rv_r^{\mathsf T}.$$
To apply $A$ to $x$: find the components $\langle x, v_i\rangle$ along the input axes, multiply them by $\sigma_i$, and use them as components along the output axes $u_i$. So $A$ maps the unit sphere of $\mathbb R^n$ onto a (possibly flattened) ellipsoid in $\mathbb R^m$ with semi-axes $\sigma_iu_i$.

Several quantities can be read off at once.

- The rank is the number of nonzero singular values; $u_1, \dots, u_r$ span the image and $v_{r+1}, \dots, v_n$ span the kernel.
- The operator norm $\|A\| = \max_{\|x\| = 1}\|Ax\|$ equals $\sigma_1$, since $\|Ax\|^2 = x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Ax \le \lambda_1\|x\|^2$ with equality at $x = v_1$.
- For square $A$, $|\det A| = \sigma_1\sigma_2\cdots\sigma_n$, because $\det U$ and $\det V$ are $\pm1$.
- For invertible square $A$, the ratio $\sigma_1/\sigma_n$ (the condition number) measures how much relative errors in $b$ can be amplified when solving $Ax = b$.

Least squares. To minimise $\|Ax - b\|$, write $y = V^{\mathsf T}x$ and $c = U^{\mathsf T}b$. Orthogonal matrices preserve length, so
$$\|Ax - b\|^2 = \|U^{\mathsf T}(U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}x - b)\|^2 = \|\Sigma y - c\|^2 = \sum_{i \le r}(\sigma_iy_i - c_i)^2 + \sum_{i > r}c_i^2.$$
This is smallest when $y_i = c_i/\sigma_i$ for $i \le r$; the $y_i$ with $i > r$ are free, and the shortest minimiser sets them to $0$. That minimiser is $x^+ = A^+b$, where $A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^{\mathsf T}$ is the pseudoinverse and $\Sigma^+$ is the $n\times m$ matrix with entries $1/\sigma_1, \dots, 1/\sigma_r$ in its first $r$ diagonal positions and zeros elsewhere. When $A$ is square and invertible, $A^+ = A^{-1}$.

blocks.title: Eckart–Young theorem
blocks.body:
Let $A = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_iu_iv_i^{\mathsf T}$ be an SVD of a real $m\times n$ matrix, set $\sigma_i = 0$ for $r < i \le \min(m, n)$, and for $0 \le k < \min(m, n)$ let $A_k = \sum_{i \le k}\sigma_iu_iv_i^{\mathsf T}$ (the truncated SVD; $A_k = A$ when $k \ge r$). Then for every $m\times n$ matrix $B$ of rank at most $k$,
$$\|A - B\| \ge \sigma_{k+1} = \|A - A_k\| \qquad\text{and}\qquad \|A - B\|_F \ge \Big(\sum_{i > k}\sigma_i^2\Big)^{1/2} = \|A - A_k\|_F,$$
where $\|M\|_F = \big(\sum_{i,j} m_{ij}^2\big)^{1/2}$ is the Frobenius norm. So $A_k$ is a best approximation of $A$ of rank at most $k$ in both the operator norm and the Frobenius norm. (The result is also called the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem.)

First, $A - A_k = \sum_{k < i \le r}\sigma_iu_iv_i^{\mathsf T}$ is itself written in SVD form, with largest singular value $\sigma_{k+1}$ (or $0$ if $k \ge r$), so $\|A - A_k\| = \sigma_{k+1}$ by the norm formula above.

Now let $\operatorname{rank}B \le k$. By rank–nullity ([[linear-maps]]), $\ker B$ has dimension at least $n - k$. The span $S$ of $v_1, \dots, v_{k+1}$ has dimension $k + 1$. Since $(n - k) + (k + 1) > n$, the two subspaces share a unit vector $x$. Write $x = \sum_{i \le k+1}c_iv_i$ with $\sum c_i^2 = 1$. Then $Bx = 0$, and
$$\|(A - B)x\|^2 = \|Ax\|^2 = \Big\|\sum_{i \le k+1}\sigma_ic_iu_i\Big\|^2 = \sum_{i \le k+1}\sigma_i^2c_i^2 \ge \sigma_{k+1}^2\sum_{i\le k+1} c_i^2 = \sigma_{k+1}^2.$$
Hence $\|A - B\| \ge \sigma_{k+1}$.

This proves the operator-norm statement. For the Frobenius norm, the equality $\|A - A_k\|_F^2 = \sigma_{k+1}^2 + \cdots + \sigma_r^2$ follows from exercise 3 below applied to $A - A_k$; the inequality for an arbitrary $B$ needs a longer argument, which we omit (see the references).

blocks.title: Low rank in practice
blocks.body:
Eckart–Young is why the SVD compresses data. A grey-scale image is an $m\times n$ matrix; storing $A_k$ needs only $k$ triples $(\sigma_i, u_i, v_i)$, that is $k(m + n + 1)$ numbers instead of $mn$. For a $1000\times 800$ image and $k = 50$ that is $90\,050$ numbers instead of $800\,000$, and because the singular values of natural images decay quickly, $A_{50}$ is often visually hard to tell apart from $A$.

The same mechanism drives principal component analysis: if the rows of $A$ are data points with the mean subtracted, then $v_1$ is the direction along which the data vary most, $v_2$ the next, and projecting onto $v_1, \dots, v_k$ is the best $k$-dimensional summary in the least-squares sense. In recommender systems a ratings matrix is approximated by a low-rank matrix, on the theory that tastes are described by a few hidden factors.

Stable algorithms avoid forming $A^{\mathsf T}A$ explicitly, because doing so squares the condition number and loses accuracy; they work on $A$ directly. For hand calculations with small matrices, however, the route through $A^{\mathsf T}A$ (or $AA^{\mathsf T}$, whichever is smaller) is the natural one.

blocks.title: A full SVD by hand
blocks.solution:
$A^{\mathsf T}A = \begin{pmatrix} 25 & 20\\ 20 & 25\end{pmatrix}$ has trace $50$ and determinant $625 - 400 = 225$, so its eigenvalues are $45$ and $5$, with unit eigenvectors $v_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1)$ and $v_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1)$. So $\sigma_1 = 3\sqrt5$ and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt5$.

Then
$$u_1 = \frac{Av_1}{\sigma_1} = \frac{(3, 9)}{\sqrt2\cdot 3\sqrt5} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(1, 3), \qquad u_2 = \frac{Av_2}{\sigma_2} = \frac{(3, -1)}{\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt5} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(3, -1),$$
which are indeed orthonormal. Hence
$$A = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3\\ 3 & -1\end{pmatrix}}_{U}\begin{pmatrix} 3\sqrt5 & 0\\ 0 & \sqrt5\end{pmatrix}\underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}}_{V^{\mathsf T}}.$$
As a check, $\sigma_1\sigma_2 = 15 = |\det A|$. Note that $A$ has eigenvalues $3$ and $5$ (it is triangular), which are not its singular values.

blocks.title: Rank-one approximation and least squares
blocks.body: Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$ and $b = (1, 2, 3)$. Find the SVD of $A$, its best rank-one approximation, and the least-squares solution of $Ax = b$.
blocks.solution:
$A^{\mathsf T}A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1\\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $4$ and $2$ with unit eigenvectors $v_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1)$ and $v_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1)$. So $\sigma_1 = 2$, $\sigma_2 = \sqrt2$, and
$$u_1 = \frac{Av_1}{2} = \frac{(2, 2, 0)}{2\sqrt2} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1, 0), \qquad u_2 = \frac{Av_2}{\sqrt2} = \frac{(0, 0, 2)}{2} = (0, 0, 1).$$
(A full $U$ needs a third vector, $u_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0)$.)

Best rank-one approximation:
$$A_1 = \sigma_1u_1v_1^{\mathsf T} = 2\cdot\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 1 & 1\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 1 & 1\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad A - A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0\\ 0 & 0\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix},$$
and $\|A - A_1\| = \sqrt2 = \sigma_2$, as Eckart–Young predicts.

Least squares: $c_1 = \langle b, u_1\rangle = \frac{3}{\sqrt2}$ and $c_2 = \langle b, u_2\rangle = 3$, so
$$x^+ = \frac{c_1}{\sigma_1}v_1 + \frac{c_2}{\sigma_2}v_2 = \frac{3}{2\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{(1,1)}{\sqrt2} + \frac{3}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{(1,-1)}{\sqrt2} = \left(\tfrac34, \tfrac34\right) + \left(\tfrac32, -\tfrac32\right) = \left(\tfrac94, -\tfrac34\right).$$
Check with the normal equations $A^{\mathsf T}Ax = A^{\mathsf T}b$: here $A^{\mathsf T}b = (6, 0)$, and $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1\\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}\left(\frac94, -\frac34\right) = (6, 0)$. The residual is $b - Ax^+ = (-\frac12, \frac12, 0)$, of length $\frac{1}{\sqrt2} = |c_3|$ with $c_3 = \langle b, u_3\rangle$.

blocks.title: Eigenvalues are trapped by singular values
blocks.body: Let $A$ be a real $n\times n$ matrix with singular values $\sigma_1 \ge \cdots \ge \sigma_n \ge 0$ (padding with zeros if the rank is less than $n$). Show that every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$, real or complex, satisfies $\sigma_n \le |\lambda| \le \sigma_1$, and that $|\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n| = \sigma_1\cdots\sigma_n$.
blocks.solution:
Let $Av = \lambda v$ with $v = a + ib \ne 0$, where $a, b$ are real vectors. Since $A$ is real, $Aa + iAb = \lambda v$, and
$$|\lambda|^2(\|a\|^2 + \|b\|^2) = \|Av\|^2 = \|Aa\|^2 + \|Ab\|^2.$$
For a real vector $x$, $\|Ax\|^2 = x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}Ax$ lies between $\sigma_n^2\|x\|^2$ and $\sigma_1^2\|x\|^2$ by the Rayleigh principle for $A^{\mathsf T}A$, whose eigenvalues are the $\sigma_i^2$. Applying this to $a$ and $b$ and adding,
$$\sigma_n^2(\|a\|^2 + \|b\|^2) \le |\lambda|^2(\|a\|^2 + \|b\|^2) \le \sigma_1^2(\|a\|^2 + \|b\|^2),$$
and dividing by $\|a\|^2 + \|b\|^2 > 0$ gives the claim. For the products, $|\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_n| = |\det A| = \sigma_1\cdots\sigma_n$.

The bounds can be far apart. For $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & t\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ both eigenvalues are $1$, but $\sigma_1 \to \infty$ and $\sigma_2 = 1/\sigma_1 \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$. Eigenvalues describe long-run behaviour of powers; singular values describe how much a single application can stretch.

blocks.body:
- Singular values are not absolute values of eigenvalues, except for symmetric (more generally, normal) matrices. $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $0, 0$ but singular values $1, 0$.
- The $u_i$ cannot be chosen independently of the $v_i$. Computing eigenvectors of $AA^{\mathsf T}$ and $A^{\mathsf T}A$ separately can produce sign mismatches; define $u_i = Av_i/\sigma_i$ instead.
- $U$ and $V$ are not unique: signs can be flipped in pairs, and for repeated singular values any orthonormal basis of the corresponding space may be used. The singular values themselves are unique.
- For an $m\times n$ matrix, $\Sigma$ has the shape $m\times n$, not square; in the compact form only the $r$ nonzero singular values and the first $r$ columns of $U$ and $V$ are kept.
- Truncating the SVD is optimal for the operator and Frobenius norms, not for every measure of error (for example, not for the largest entry of $A - B$: for $A = \operatorname{diag}(2, 1)$ and $k = 1$ the truncated SVD leaves an entry $1$, while a suitable rank-one $B$ makes every entry of $A - B$ smaller than $0.75$).

The SVD is the [[spectral-theorem|spectral theorem]] applied to $A^{\mathsf T}A$, and it refines [[linear-maps|rank–nullity]] by giving orthonormal bases of the image and kernel at once. It solves overdetermined and underdetermined [[linear-systems]] in the least-squares sense, and the ratio $\sigma_1/\sigma_n$ is the standard measure of how sensitive such a system is to errors. For square $A$, $|\det A| = \prod \sigma_i$ (see [[determinants]]).

In statistics the SVD of a centred data matrix with $N$ rows (one per observation) gives the principal components: uncorrelated linear combinations of the variables ([[random-variables]]) with sample variances $\sigma_i^2/(N-1)$. Low-rank approximation is also used in latent semantic indexing of documents and in collaborative filtering. The polar decomposition $A = (UV^{\mathsf T})(V\Sigma V^{\mathsf T})$, writing a square matrix as an orthogonal matrix (a rotation, possibly combined with a reflection) times a symmetric positive semidefinite stretch, is an immediate corollary.

1. Find the singular values of $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.
2. Show that the singular values of a real symmetric matrix are the absolute values of its eigenvalues.
3. Show that the Frobenius norm satisfies $\|A\|_F^2 = \sigma_1^2 + \cdots + \sigma_r^2$. (Hint: $\|A\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}A)$.)
4. Find the shortest solution of the single equation $x + 2y + 2z = 9$ using the pseudoinverse.
